cia-0000104916:
India: A Growing Role in Technology Transfer is a CIA memorandum released as declassified document 0000104916, dated May 5, 1985 in the catalog. The sample memorandum is dated June 7, 1985, a month later. It came from the Office of Near East and South Asia Analysis in the Directorate of Intelligence.

The summary says Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi had introduced sweeping economic reforms. Those reforms promised to encourage imports of sophisticated western technology. They also promised to boost India's ability to manufacture its own high-tech products. As a result, India would offer a more attractive target for Soviet science and technology collectors.
cia-0000119216:
Dated November 3, 1967, this CIA document covers the detention of American prisoners of war in Hanoi. By then, North Vietnam's capital held many captured American airmen in its prisons. The best known of those prisons was later nicknamed the Hanoi Hilton by the men held there.

The document records what the agency knew about how and where the prisoners were confined. Such reporting fed decisions in Washington about protests, talks, and public pressure over prisoner treatment. It also forms part of the wartime record of a captivity that lasted years for many men, written while their fate was still unknown to their families.
cia-0000119716:
Dated September 1956, this CIA paper examines probable developments in Eastern Europe and what they would mean for Soviet policy. Poland and Hungary were both in turmoil that autumn. Moscow's hold on its allies suddenly looked less certain than it had in years.

The paper steps back from single countries to the empire as a whole. It asks how unrest at the edges might force choices at the center: reform, concession, or force. That framing gives the paper lasting interest. Written weeks before the Hungarian Revolution, it shows analysts thinking through the Soviet dilemma that the uprising would soon pose in its sharpest form.
cia-0000132416: Cuban developments return as item 15 in the CIA's Latin America series, dated November 1, 1959. The numbered format shows Cuba becoming a standing item on the agency's agenda. Two months had passed since the last general survey in the file. The short item updates the picture, tracking the new regime's latest moves for readers who followed the series as a running watch.
cia-0000132616: The situation in Cuba fills item 2 of the CIA's Latin America series, dated July 4, 1960. Eighteen months into the revolution, that situation was the standing question before the agency. By the middle of 1960 the answer grew darker with each passing month. The short item gives the current picture as analysts summed it up for their readers that summer.
cia-0000135816: Dated 2 May 1954, a declassified CIA document deals with an operational report with five attachments, its key names blank or deleted in the heading. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000135916: about January 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about a cable from Sherwood to Lincoln listing targets, one coded station writing to another. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136116: A CIA cable dated 5 April 1954 deals with procedures for CADICK, sent soonest, joined to a statement that the heading cuts off, in files since declassified. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136216: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 1 May 1954, covers Instruction 3 about a shipment of Swiss goods, the cargo cut off in the heading, for LANGEVIN. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000137316: Cuba shows a real threat of extremist control, this CIA briefing concludes. It served the 421st National Security Council meeting on 29 October 1959. There is almost no hope Castro can be swayed. He will not moderate his course. He will not recognize the danger of communism. He relies almost wholly on leftist advisers. Last week he spoke bluntly. If they want to call us communists, let them, he said. Raul Castro now heads all police and military forces. Che Guevara runs industrial planning.

The panel's first big task: work out a fair scale for how member states should split the costs of the UN, in time for the next part of the session.
un-ga-res-a-69-16:
Ten years for people of African descent were proclaimed by the General Assembly in 2013, and Resolution A/69/16 sets that decade in motion. The span runs from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2024. Its theme is named in full: people of African descent, with the watchwords of respect, justice, and growth. The start of the decade falls right after the main debate of the Assembly's sixty-ninth session.

The text recalls the world year for people of African descent, kept in 2011. Gains won in that year form the base for the decade's work. Joint force is the aim: the decade should add fresh weight to the fight against racism in all its forms, and to the pledges of the Durban meeting of 2001.
un-sc-res-1416: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 1416 is catalogued here as dating from 2002. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1516:
Resolution 1516 came in November 2003, days after truck bombs struck synagogues and British targets in Istanbul, Turkey. The Security Council used it to condemn those attacks in the strongest terms. Dozens of people had been killed and hundreds hurt in the blasts.

Beyond the condemnation, the members call on all states to help find and punish those behind the bombings. They also repeat that terrorism threatens world peace and must be fought under the UN Charter. Short as it is, the text shows the Council's standard response to a major terror attack in those years.
un-sc-res-1616: Formal output of the Security Council, Resolution 1616 survives in this collection in official-record wording from Wikisource. Many resolutions adjust running machinery: a mission renewed, a sanctions list updated, a deadline moved. The text here follows the usual architecture for such acts, and its exact terms are what officials on the ground would have followed.
un-sc-res-2016: Under number 2016, a Security Council decision is preserved in this collection through a Wikisource copy of the UN record. The text observes the genre's discipline: the preamble argues, the operative part acts, and neither does the other's job. Keeping both parts together and complete is what makes the entry a faithful piece of the record.
cia-0000132516:
Paired with a same-day companion, this CIA paper on Cuba is dated April 4, 1961. Intelligence was flowing to the White House daily by then. The Bay of Pigs landing, planned in secret, was thirteen days away.

Two papers on one day, so close to the operation, show the tempo of the final countdown. Each fed the pre-invasion picture that planners relied on: conditions on the island as the exile force readied itself. Read together with its companion, the briefing helps reconstruct what Washington thought it knew in April 1961. The pair of papers is preserved together in this record.
cia-0000135616: One of the Spanish-language records of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 5 February 1961. The brigade of Cuban exiles, trained and supplied by the CIA, landed in Cuba two months later. February found it in final training. The catalog gives this item no subject heading. It is described only by date, language, and provenance. The piece is part of the brigade's declassified paperwork, preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000136616: A Spanish document dated 1 January 1961 survives in the 2506 Brigade files. The New Year found the brigade of Cuban exiles in CIA-run training, three months from the landing that would make it famous. The catalog record names no subject for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish, one of the brigade's records from the start of its final year-quarter, released with the rest of the declassified archive.
plos-pone-0000016:
Yang Zhou, Hao Wu, Shuai Li, and co-authors reported in 2006 on a protein the brain needs to lock in lasting memories. Long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of a connection between nerve cells, and its late phase is what turns a fresh impression into a durable memory. The hippocampus, a deep brain structure, is central to that process.

The team showed that TORC1, a protein that helps switch on memory-related genes, is required for the late phase to hold in the hippocampus. Block that step, and the strengthening fades. The result connects memory storage to gene activity inside the cell, and it points at a control point that later memory research keeps returning to.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d16: President Roosevelt wrote to Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek on June 30, 1943, closing the month's run of summit letters. The message is Document 16 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang led China's war against Japan and pressed Washington steadily for aid and standing. Five months later he would meet Roosevelt and Churchill at Cairo. The record gives the date and the names; the letter's own text carries the rest.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d116: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on November 11, 1943, the day before he boarded the Iowa for the Atlantic crossing. The letter is Document 116 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. He would be at sea, largely in radio silence, for the next ten days, which gave the last letters extra weight. The record gives the date and the names. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d216:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent a secret, urgent telegram to Harry Hopkins in Washington on 13 November 1943. Only part of the message is printed here; the rest appears earlier in the volume. The surviving part turns to the Soviet request for Italian ships, still unanswered.

Harriman notes that no reply had come to Secretary Hull's message of 2 November on the ships. Molotov was keen to know what was being done to act on the favorable American reaction. He guesses Molotov would be content to hear the matter would be discussed at Cairo, though that might lead him to bring a naval officer along to argue the Soviet case.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d316:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy wrote to Harry Hopkins at Cairo on 25 November 1943, a long memorandum on civil affairs in occupied territory. He had missed his chance to brief Hopkins at lunch, with Lord Leathers present, and so puts his warning in writing instead.

Churchill, strongly briefed, means to raise the subject with Roosevelt soon. He will press the Foreign Office line. It calls for civilian administrators following the forward zone. It also calls for a combined civil affairs committee working from London rather than through Washington. McCloy reports that the British chiefs, and Sir John Dill, in fact side with the American view. His attachments argue that London has spent months pulling occupation policy decisions to itself and has frustrated the joint committee, leaving the work at an impasse.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d416:
Elmer Davis, director of the Office of War Information, sent a secret, rapid telegram from Washington on 4 December 1943. It went to Wallace Carroll, his London bureau chief. It carried a message for Brendan Bracken, the British minister of information. It follows Moscow's early announcement of the Tehran Conference.

Now that the Russians have set us both back on our tails, Davis writes, perhaps the two governments can agree on measures to stop such deplorable incidents repeating. He has asked the State Department to inquire in Moscow how the Russian announcement happened and whether it broke an agreed release date. On Senator Connally's speech, he judges the senator said nothing beyond the Reuters Lisbon story and the week's speculation. The tail of the message, for Carroll alone, is wry: sorry you have had to take the heat in the front line.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d516:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt in Ankara wrote to Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on December 10, 1943. Ambassador-to-ambassador letters, bypassing both capitals, were a valued channel in wartime diplomacy. The State Department printed this one in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Steinhardt held the Turkish post and Harriman the Soviet one, and Turkey's choices touched Russia directly, from the Straits to the Black Sea. A direct exchange between the two men joined up American policy at two of its most sensitive points. For readers, the letter shows senior envoys coordinating among themselves in the days when the Cairo talks with Turkey were still fresh.
frus-1944-quebec-d16:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on July 17, 1944, the day after Churchill's two messages. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, in the correspondence that led to the September conference.

Roosevelt's replies that summer defended the agreed strategy, above all the invasion of southern France, against British second thoughts. His letters combined personal warmth with a firmness that reflected America's growing weight in the coalition. For readers, this message shows the President managing his most important ally in writing, at the height of the campaign in France and on the road to Quebec.
frus-1944-quebec-d116:
Rudolf Schoenfeld, the American chargé near the Polish government in exile in London, cabled this report to Washington on September 2, 1944. It relays a broadcast by Polish Prime Minister Stanisław Mikołajczyk, marking five years since Germany attacked Poland. His message was aimed at the fighters holding out in Warsaw.

Mikołajczyk defended the decision to rise in the open and appealed directly to Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill for help. Warsaw is waiting, he told them, and the whole Polish nation with it. He admitted the fighters had not received the aid they were owed, despite brave supply flights. He promised to say so publicly if no help came.
frus-1944-quebec-d216:
Morgenthau dictated this draft at Quebec on September 15, 1944, after withdrawing with Cherwell to put the agreed position on Germany in writing. It records Churchill summing up the discussion on the Ruhr and the Saar. Russia and other allies could help themselves to whatever machinery they wished. The two districts' industries would be shut down under an international body.

That body would supervise the Ruhr and Saar to see the industries did not start up again. The program, the draft says, formed part of a plan for diverting Germany into largely an agricultural country. The endorsement marks it "Draft 1." Churchill found this version unacceptable and dictated his own, which both leaders initialed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d16: Stalin's answer to Roosevelt came on 29 October 1944, five days after the president's last message. Preserved as document 16 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, it continues the paired exchange the Office of the Historian printed in order. These letters matter because the two men rarely met, so written messages carried trust, pressure, and warning between them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d116:
Harry Dexter White, assistant to the Secretary of the Treasury, wrote this file memorandum on the Quebec aftermath. It records a meeting in Secretary Hull's office on 20 September 1944, with Stimson, Morgenthau, and officials of three departments present. The memo is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Hull opened in anger over a leaked account of a meeting at Sumner Welles's home, complaining that Welles seemed to run a second State Department. Morgenthau then told, in detail, how the German question had run at Quebec. He handed Hull and Stimson copies of the memorandum on Germany that Roosevelt and Churchill had initialed there. The paper catches a cabinet split in the open, days after the Quebec Conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d216:
French opinion on Germany was divided, and this briefing book paper maps it party by party. “French Views on the Treatment of Germany,” dated 1 January 1945, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It was prepared for the President's trip to the Big Three talks.

A large share of the French, perhaps a majority, still holds that some Germans are not beyond saving. A purged and chastened Germany, on this view, must in time regain a weighty place in Europe. The Socialists hold it most steadily, though with few illusions. The Communists tend to sort Germans into good and bad. The Christian Democrats stand near Bidault: Germany is not to be enslaved, but she must be made unable to wage another war. Dismemberment draws its strength from conservative circles.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d316:
Writing to President Roosevelt from Malta on January 30, 1945, the Joint Chiefs of Staff raised a worry about Allied aims. They recalled that Harry Hopkins and Richard Law had urged both governments to prepare advice on shipping for freed areas. That advice was meant for the coming conference.

Twice, the memo says, the British chiefs had been asked to restate the shared goal. That goal was the fastest possible surrender of Germany and Japan, beating Germany first while pressing Japan hard. Twice the British had attached conditions to their answer. The paper warns the President, in plain terms, that a basic point of strategy was still not settled.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d416:
Three governments speak with one voice in this British draft message to Tito and Subasic, dated February 9, 1945. The heads of the three powers, it says, have met and talked over the Yugoslav question. They advise that the Tito-Subasic pact be put into force at once. A new government should be formed on its basis.

Once formed, the government should declare two things. The AVNOJ body would be widened with members of the old Skupstina who had not stained themselves, forming a short-term parliament. And the laws passed by AVNOJ would be put to a later assembly for approval. The draft shows the West bargaining for free rule by decree.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d16:
A formidable deployment might settle Venezia Giulia without fighting, Churchill argued to Truman on May 21, 1945. If the Western deployment stayed strong, he thought, a solution could be reached. A firm attitude there would also be of value in the coming discussions with Stalin. The need for the triple meeting at the earliest moment, he repeated, was very great.

A British election campaign would run during June, he noted, but all parties agreed on foreign policy, so no postponement was needed. He asked Truman for any idea of date and place, so the two could make their several requests to Stalin. He feared Stalin might play for time, to remain all powerful in Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d116:
The secretary of the Joint Chiefs of Staff sent Berlin the final roster of the chiefs' party on July 3, 1945. The telegram to liaison officer Colonel Lowry is document 116 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It names the officers who would join General Parks's advance group already in Berlin.

The list is headed by the chiefs themselves: General Marshall for the Army, Admiral King for the Navy, and General Arnold for the air forces. Around them are deputies, planners, and staff officers, down through colonels, warrant officers, and yeomen. Even after both sides agreed to keep staffs small, the American military party ran to dozens of named men. The telegram is a roll call of the top American command team of the Second World War.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d216:
Ambassador Winant reported a British decision to hold back peace treaty proposals in extracts dated July 13, 1945. The extracts form document 216 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Foreign Office had answered American messages urging strong pressure over the Balkan satellites and opposing early peace treaties with their present governments.

In view of the State Department's opinions, the Foreign Office says, it has not put its proposals to the Soviet government in advance of the conference, as it had intended. It may, however, wish to put them forward at the conference itself. The proposals concerned peace treaties with Bulgaria, Hungary, and Romania. The exchange shows London falling in with Washington's wish to keep the satellite question for the leaders' table.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d316:
John Hickerson of the State Department recorded a talk with a British diplomat in a memorandum dated July 14, 1945. Paul Gore-Booth, first secretary at the British Embassy, had come in the day before at his own request. He admitted one point in the American attitude toward Bulgaria and Rumania still puzzled him.

The question was whether Washington meant to delay recognition and peace treaties until those governments were reorganized. British officials, the memo suggests, hoped to persuade the United States toward early recognition instead. Hickerson's note catches the allies testing each other's bottom lines on the eve of Potsdam, each unsure how firm the other stood.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d416:
McCloy's doubts reach Winant in a Washington cable of July 14, 1945. It paraphrases McCloy's telegram of July 11. The Assistant Secretary of War asks that American sanction be postponed. The sanction would cover the suggested instructions to allied representatives, on the added requirements set out in the declaration of June 5. He wants a chance to discuss the matter first.

McCloy sees the document as negative in character. It may create confusion, he warns, because men may read it in different ways. The term allied representative is nowhere clearly defined, either in meaning or in use. A single zone commander might act on matters meant for the allies acting jointly. That risk grows where the Control Council has not agreed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d516:
Washington corrects Zhukov in Grew's urgent cable to Murphy of July 9, 1945. With respect to the Marshal's statement that the Crimea Conference established the Polish frontier along the Oder and Neisse rivers, Grew writes, we can only comment that he has been misinformed. At Crimea it was agreed that Poland should later receive an increase of territory in the west.

This government, he stresses, has not accepted any specific line, and has not agreed to a date for the transfer of German territory to Poland. Deputy Commissar Vyshinsky's letter of May 16 to Harriman confirms the American reading: final determination of Poland's western boundary will be made at the peace settlement, as the Crimea agreement envisaged.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d616:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded a talk with French ambassador Henri Bonnet in a memo dated June 25, 1945. Extracts form document 616 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The subject was the souring state of relations between the United States and France.

Bonnet said he came without instructions, moved by his duty to keep the two states close. Both he and General de Gaulle, he said, earnestly wished for closer ties. Yet the trend ran the other way, since France had won little satisfaction on a string of issues. French public opinion, he warned, was turning in a way that hurt the friendship. One sore point he named was a corps for the Far East. Washington had agreed in talks with Bidault that a French army corps could go east. It would fight Japan, but nothing more had been heard of it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-16:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 18, 1945, record the Allied chiefs' afternoon session at Potsdam. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Four decisions are set out in the part printed here.

The chiefs first approved the conclusions of their 194th meeting, with one wording change on a corps commander's dispatch to the Pacific. They then approved a memo on French and Dutch participation in the war against Japan. The secretaries were directed to forward it to the French and Netherlands representatives separately. Staff conversations with Portugal were approved next, in the form of a letter to the two foreign ministries. The chiefs then turned to Southeast Asia and the Southwest Pacific. General Marshall opened that debate by questioning the British chiefs on their paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-116:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sat again at Potsdam on July 26, 1945, and these minutes record the session. That day the conference paused its normal rhythm around the British election results. Military work went on all the same. The war in the Pacific still demanded daily choices from the chiefs assembled in Germany.

Minutes of the chiefs show strategy stated in short, hard terms. They list the facts officers trusted and the risks they flagged. Readers can see how advice hardened into plans for the President. Printed in the second Potsdam volume, the record ties the military track to the talks of the same hours.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d716:
Patrick Hurley, the ambassador in China, answered the Secretary of State on July 28, 1945. Document 716 continues the Byrnes-Hurley exchange printed in the second Potsdam volume. Hurley reported from Chungking, the wartime capital. His post placed him between China's government and its Communist rivals, with Japan still in the field.

An ambassador's reply carries ground truth. Hurley could say what Potsdam's choices would mean where he stood. Readers get the view from a hard post at a strained time. The letter shows how the conference's reach touched allies far from Germany. It also marks Hurley's direct line to the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d816:
Byrnes wrote directly to Melbourne in Rumania on July 25, 1945, in document 816. The Secretary of State addressed his acting representative in Bucharest from Potsdam. A secretary's own letter to a small post was a strong signal. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Direct guidance from the top steadied a mission under strain. Melbourne could quote the Secretary's line in Bucharest. Readers see the summit reaching down to a hard-pressed desk. The document also shows Rumania's weight in Byrnes's mind at the midpoint. Of all the Balkan files, hers drew the chief's own hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d916:
The United States put this proposal on reparations and related matters before the Potsdam talks on July 23, 1945. It claims the backing of the Allied Commission on Reparations. Under the plan, available reparations would be shared among claimant nations by war burden, losses, and part in victory.

Each occupying power could remove capital equipment, current goods, and stocks from its own zone. Removals must first end Germany's war-making power and speed recovery in ruined lands. Set dates would end the taking: capital equipment by May 10, 1947, and stocks and current goods by May 10, 1951. A restitution section follows, listing loot that must be returned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1016:
Soviet delegates handed this proposal on trying the main war criminals to the American and British delegations on July 30, 1945. It calls for an international tribunal, set up soon, for leaders whose crimes had no single place. That test comes from the Moscow Declaration of November 1, 1943.

Ten names are listed for first judgment: Goering, Hess, Ribbentrop, Ley, Keitel, Doenitz, Kaltenbrunner, Frick, Streicher, and Krupp. The paper also declares that the three Allied governments will use every means to win surrender of war criminals hiding in neutral lands. If a neutral state refuses, the three will consult on steps to enforce their decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1116:
For the second time in the summit's run, the Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Kirk in Italy on 27 July 1945. Ten days into the Potsdam Conference, Washington was still handling the Italian file with care. The stream of cables to Rome never slowed.

Italy mattered to the settlement in its own right. Its treaty and its new state could not wait for the German talks to end. Each message to Kirk adjusted orders or sought fresh word from the ground. This dispatch is one beat in a steady two-way rhythm. It shows a major embassy being run in step with a summit.
pmc-13457116: Some inflammatory bowel disease patients do not fit neatly into Crohn's or ulcerative colitis and get labeled unclassified. Analyzing gut tissue gene signatures, the authors argue that IBD-unclassified is actually its own distinct subtype, marked by a three-gene pattern. A molecular definition would end the diagnostic limbo and guide subtype-specific treatment.
pmc-13458916: Rheumatic fever can scar the mitral valve until it barely opens, a condition called mitral stenosis. This paper covers balloon mitral valvotomy, the catheter procedure that cracks the narrowed valve open from inside. For patients in regions where rheumatic disease is common, it is a less invasive lifeline than open-heart surgery.
pmc-13343316: Doctors are asked to care for patients' spirits as well as their bodies, but medical schools rarely teach how. This paper examines efforts to integrate spiritual care teaching into the Australian medical curriculum. The analysis shows what it takes to make future doctors comfortable with the sacred.
pmc-13430216: Cancer drugs can trigger skin reactions driven by eosinophils, forcing patients to stop life-saving therapy. This phase II trial tested benralizumab, an eosinophil-depleting antibody, for these cutaneous adverse events. The results explore whether calming the skin lets patients stay on their cancer treatment.
pmc-13399116: Prostate cancers that resist hormone therapy need new targets. Evaluating patient tissue, the authors identified B7-H3 as an androgen-regulated, broadly expressed target suitable for combination therapy. The widely expressed marker could anchor the next generation of prostate cancer drugs, including antibody and combination approaches.
pmc-13468216: Fructans and fructooligosaccharides sweeten plants and feed beneficial gut bacteria. This review covers their metabolism, functional roles in plants and fruits, and emerging biotechnological opportunities. The carbohydrate chemistry connects plant biology to human nutrition, spanning metabolism, functional food roles, and biotech applications.
pmc-13439016: Brief and organizational: this is the special issue front matter for the IUNS-ICN Paris 2025 nutrition congress. Rather than research, it frames the collection of papers. The issue gathers the field's latest thinking on global nutrition science and policy from the Paris congress.
pmc-13421916: Two related plant groups took opposite paths across the tropics. This study showed how contrasting dispersal histories shaped distinct evolutionary trajectories between Malesian and pantropical Talipariti. The comparison reveals how geography writes different evolutionary stories from similar tropical beginnings across different island geographies.
pmc-13530716: Conference poster: the authors tracked the chronological progression of pain and muscle fiber damage in a novel exercise-induced muscle injury model. The time-course data maps how muscle injury evolves after strenuous exercise. Presented as a research poster. The model provides a controlled way to study muscle damage and recovery.
pmc-13530816: Professional hockey is fast and violent, and injury patterns matter for prevention. This poster mapped the epidemiology of NHL injuries from 2012 to 2023 in a retrospective analysis. The decade of data reveals how the modern game injures its players.
pmc-13549216: Microlaryngoscopy requires a clear view of the vocal cords, but some patients are anatomically difficult. This scoping review examined prediction of difficult laryngeal exposure. The synthesis helps surgeons anticipate trouble and plan accordingly. Better prediction means safer airway surgery for difficult cases.
pmc-13513816: Black soldier fly larvae can convert waste into protein-rich animal feed. The authors tested how substrate composition affects bioconversion efficiency and nutritional quality of Hermetia illucens larvae in tropical conditions. The results optimize insect farming for sustainable feed production. Optimized insect farming supports sustainable protein production.
pmc-13401616: Biological age, how old the body acts versus the calendar, can be read in blood proteins. The authors constructed and validated a plasma protein-based musculoskeletal biological age, exploring genetic and environmental influences. The protein clock could flag accelerated musculoskeletal aging before symptoms appear.
pmc-13507516: Sulfur dioxide pollution burns the lungs, and anti-inflammatory treatments are limited. In mice, the authors showed intratracheal interleukin-10 reduces acute lung injury from sulfur dioxide exposure. The local cytokine delivery offers a targeted approach to chemical lung injury. Targeted cytokine therapy may help victims of air pollution.
pmc-13495116: DNA damage at specific spots can cause the mutations that drive cancer. The authors showed DNA-peptide crosslinks at codon 249 of p53 induce G-to-A transitions. The site-specific chemistry illuminates how a key tumor suppressor gets disabled. Understanding mutagenesis informs cancer prevention.
pmc-13493216: Classifying ovarian tumors from ultrasound is challenging with limited labeled data. STL-DeepBDC is a robust few-shot learning framework for multiclass classification. The AI approach learns from few examples, suiting real-world clinical data scarcity. AI learns to diagnose from scarce data.

dunsany-last-book-of-wonder-1916:

lodge-raymond-1916:

A cook on the steamer first puts serious reading into his hands. The volume covers his teens among cooks, clerks, and outcasts. It stands as one of the great records of a self-made education.
lombard-sententiae-quaracchi-1916:
Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, compiled his Four Books of Sentences in the 1150s, and the work became the textbook of theology for the Latin West. Every master, from Aquinas to Luther, had to lecture on it. The text here is the critical edition of the College of Saint Bonaventure at Quaracchi, 1916, in two volumes and in Latin.

The books move from God and the Trinity to creation, then to Christ and the virtues, and last to the sacraments and the end of the world. Lombard weaves the church fathers into one ordered web of questions. No English version in the public domain exists. To read the Sentences is to read the syllabus of the medieval schools.
procopius-wars-vandalic-dewing-1916:
Books three and four of the History of the Wars of Procopius tell how Belisarius won North Africa back from the Vandals. H. B. Dewing's Loeb translation of 1916 carries the text. Procopius sailed with the fleet in 533 and saw the campaign himself. His post as the general's secretary gave him the council tent view.

The fleet lands, the Vandals fall at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, and Carthage opens its gates. Then the hard part starts: Moorish wars, mutinies, and a province that would not stay won. Procopius tells it with a soldier's eye for ground and luck. The Vandal kingdom, a century old, vanishes in a year of his telling.
procopius-wars-gothic-1-dewing-1916:
The Gothic War of Procopius opens in books five and six, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1916. Justinian sent Belisarius to take Italy back from the Ostrogoths, and Procopius went with him as his secretary. This first half of the war runs through the great siege of Rome.

Naples falls, Rome is taken, lost in siege, and held against the Gothic king Vitiges in a year of sorties and starvation. Procopius gives the war street by street and wall by wall. He also pauses for the plague winds and the strange signs of the age. The volume is the fullest battle narrative to survive from the ancient world.
al-baladhuri-origins-islamic-state-hitti:
Al-Baladhuri, a scholar at the Abbasid court in the ninth century, wrote the Futuh al-Buldan, the Book of the Conquests of the Lands. Philip Hitti translated the first part into English in 1916 at Columbia. It is the chief early Arabic account of how the caliphate's armies took the Middle East.

Country by country, al-Baladhuri tells how each land fell or made terms: Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Persia, and the islands. He names the treaties, the taxes set, and the men who led the armies. His sources were the records and reports of the caliph's own administration. Scholars start with him for the shape of the early Islamic state.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-5-:
The fifth and last volume of Maudslay's Bernal Díaz, from 1916, closes The True History of the Conquest of New Spain. Díaz's chronicle, written in 1568 and printed in 1632, ends with the campaigns that followed the fall of Mexico. Appendices and an index complete the Hakluyt Society edition.

An old soldier's memory governs the whole work, and its last pages keep his plain, stubborn voice. Díaz never stops insisting that common men, not only Cortés, won New Spain. Paired with Cortés's own letters, his history lets readers judge the conquest from two sides of the same camp. The set remains the fullest soldier's account of that world-changing war.
diderot-early-philosophical-works-jourda:
Denis Diderot, before the great Encyclopédie made his name, wrote the bold little works gathered here. Margaret Jourdain's translation, issued by Open Court in 1916, holds the Philosophic Thoughts of 1746 and the Letter on the Blind of 1749, with its later Addition. The Letter on the Deaf and Dumb of 1751 completes the set.

The Thoughts are sharp sparks on God, nature, and the passions, in the manner of Shaftesbury. The Letter on the Blind asks how a man born blind builds a world, and lands its author in prison for his answers. In the Letter on the Deaf and Dumb, Diderot turns to language and gesture. Together they show a first-rate mind finding its weapons.
boutroux-contingency-laws-nature-1916:
French thinker Emile Boutroux published De la contingence des lois de la nature in 1874, early in his career. Fred Rothwell's English translation followed in 1916. The short work attacks a belief most scientists of the day took for granted. It holds that the laws of nature had to be as they are.

Boutroux argues the opposite: those laws are contingent, meaning they could have been otherwise. Each level of nature, from matter to life to mind, brings something new that lower levels cannot predict. His case gave French spiritualism one of its founding texts. It still frames debate on chance, freedom, and natural order.
barrow-geometrical-lectures-child-1916:
Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher at Cambridge, gave his Geometrical Lectures in the years before Newton rose. J. M. Child translated the Latin Lectiones geometricae for Open Court in 1916. Barrow treats curves, tangents, and areas with pure geometry. Along the way he comes close to the fundamental theorem of calculus.

That theorem links tangents and areas as inverse operations, the core of calculus. Barrow states a form of it in geometric dress. Child's notes help readers track the proofs and their later echoes. The lectures show calculus in the moment before its birth. Newton learned from the man who wrote them. Historians of math prize the text highly.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol16:
By 1874 the Journal of Discourses reached Volume XVI, still printed at Liverpool from shorthand reports. Brigham Young and the senior elders address the Saints on doctrine and the duties of their gathered life. The sermons preserve not just what was taught, but how it sounded from the pulpit.

Sixteen volumes in, the set had become the movement's memory of its own mind. A reader can watch themes return year after year, each time fitted to new needs. Volume XVI holds that pattern steady, one more link in the running doctrinal record of the Latter-day Saints.
shaker-testimonies-mother-ann-lee-1816:
Those who knew Mother Ann Lee best set down their memories in the Testimonies of 1816, reprinted here in the 1888 edition. Elders and sisters recall the Shaker foundress's life, sayings, sufferings, and revelations. Their witness accounts form the movement's first hagiography, written within living memory of its subject.

Hardship in England, passage to America, and the first hard years of the community pass through these pages. The speakers testify rather than argue, swearing to what they saw and heard. For anyone studying Shaker beginnings, this stands as the primary source, the foundress preserved by her own people.
boas-tsimshian-mythology-1916:
Franz Boas, the founder of modern American anthropology, built this 1916 study from texts dictated by Henry Tate, a Tsimshian man of the northern Northwest Coast. Boas printed the myths as Tate told them, with close translation, in a Bureau of American Ethnology report.

The tales include the Raven cycle, in which the trickster steals light and shapes the world, and crest myths that families treated as treasured property. Boas added analysis showing how the stories link to Tsimshian social rank and custom. The book is a landmark of text-based fieldwork, preserving a people's own telling of their traditions.
yeats-reveries-1916:
Yeats looked back at his own beginnings in this 1916 autobiography, covering his childhood in Sligo and his youth in London. It is the first of his prose memoirs and the root of much of his later myth-making about himself.

He recalls his grandfather's house by the sea, the servants' tales of fairies, and the Sligo landscape that filled his imagination. In London he meets the poets and occultists who formed his early circle. The writing is tender and exact, already shaping memory into symbol. Readers of the poems will find here the places and people behind them, in the poet's own prose.
pound-gaudier-brzeska-1916:
Henri Gaudier-Brzeska was a French sculptor working in London, a leader of the vorticist movement, who was killed in the trenches in 1915 at twenty-three. Ezra Pound, his friend and champion, published this memoir and manifesto in 1916.

Pound prints Gaudier's letters from the front, his statements on art, and his own fierce defense of the young sculptor's work. The book is part biography, part battle cry for the new art of hard, clear form. Grief drives it: Pound is building a monument in print for a friend the war erased. It remains vorticism's founding document.
lawrence-twilight-italy-1916:
Lawrence wrote these travel sketches after walking and staying around Lake Garda in the years before the First World War. Twilight in Italy, published in 1916, collects them into his first travel book.

He describes peasants, priests, dancers, and lemon gardens with a poet's eye and a prophet's temper. Again and again he sets the old, bodily life of Italy against the machine age creeping over it. The sketches wander, argue, and suddenly blaze into description of light and water. It is travel writing as thinking aloud, and it began a form Lawrence made his own.
lawrence-amores-1916:
Amores, published in 1916, is Lawrence's third book of poems and the first from the years of his marriage to Frieda. The love poems gathered here are fierce and tender by turns, written out of the couple's early life together.

Lawrence writes of desire, quarrels, longing, and the strange peace two people find in each other. The verse is looser than his apprentice work, feeling its way toward the free forms he would later master. Some poems still wear the dress of older lyric styles. Taken together, they show a poet remaking himself inside a marriage that changed his life and art.
russell-social-reconstruction-1916:
Principles of Social Reconstruction, published in 1916, is Russell's wartime program for rebuilding society, and it cost him his Cambridge lectureship. Written as Britain conscripted its young men, the book asks what a good society would actually protect.

Russell sets impulse, the urge to grow and create, against the dead hand of possession and power. He applies the test to the state, war, property, marriage, and schooling. His standard is simple: institutions are good when they help human beings grow. The book made him a hero to reformers and a marked man to the authorities of his day.
royce-hope-great-community-1916:
The Hope of the Great Community, published in 1916, gathers Royce's wartime addresses on the hope of a world community beyond nationalism. Dying that year, he spent his last public efforts arguing that the war's horror might teach mankind its interdependence.

Royce proposes that the duties of loyalty, learned in small communities, can extend to a great community of mankind, bound by interpretation and mutual understanding. He addresses America's role with both pride and warning. The addresses are brief and valedictory in feeling. The book stands as the final word of a philosopher who made community his life's theme.
collingwood-religion-philosophy-1916:
Religion and Philosophy, published in 1916, is R. G. Collingwood's early study of how religious faith and philosophical reason relate. He wrote it while a young Oxford tutor, before the work on history that made his name.

Collingwood argues that religion and philosophy are not rivals but overlapping forms of thought, each expressing man's attempt to grasp his world whole. Where they conflict, he seeks the common ground of experience beneath doctrine and system. The book is earnest and exploratory, a young thinker's first map. Readers of his later work will find the seeds of his philosophy of history here.
plos-pone-0003416:
Guadalupe Gómez-Baena and co-authors studied sugar use by an ocean microbe in this 2008 paper. Prochlorococcus is a tiny sea bacterium that lives by photosynthesis. It was long treated as feeding on sunlight and air alone. No one had directly tested whether it can take up sugars.

The team used strains adapted to bright light and to dim light. Both could take up glucose from the water around them. Glucose also changed which genes the cells switched on. The result blurs the line between pure plant-like feeding and a more mixed diet.
plos-pone-0003516:
Shen Yin and co-authors studied chromosome sorting in mouse eggs for this 2008 paper. Meiosis halves chromosome counts to make eggs and sperm. Partner chromosomes part in the first division, sister copies in the second. Why sisters stay joined during the first round was the question.

A protein called Shugoshin1 appears to guard that join. Its role covers both partner separation and sister handling in oocytes. Losing such a guard would scramble the divisions. The work clarifies a choreography every gamete depends on. Egg errors are a leading cause of failed births in mammals.
plos-pone-0003616:
Alessandra Bandera and co-authors studied immune recovery after stem cell transplants in this 2008 paper. Autologous transplants return a patient's own blood stem cells. CD4 helper T cell counts stay low for a time afterward. Unlike in HIV, opportunistic infections stay uncommon in these patients.

The team found fully competent CD8 T lymphocytes present in recipients. Those killer cells worked despite an ineffectual T-helper response. Working killers may explain the missing infections. The result separates cell counts from true immune function. Stem cell grafts are now standard care for many blood cancers.
plos-pone-0003716:
Chun-Hong Zhu, Jinyong Kim, Jerry W. Shay, and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. When cells are stressed, they park stalled protein-making machinery in blobs called stress granules. A screen for genes that protect human muscle cells from oxidative stress turned up a new protein, SGNP.

SGNP sits in both stress granules and the nucleolus, the cell's ribosome factory. The evidence ties it to the handling and transport of 5.8S ribosomal RNA. The finding links the cell's emergency depots with the making of its protein factories, two systems usually studied apart.
plos-pone-0003816:
Ha Tran, Huaiyang Chen, Andreas Walz, and colleagues published this smell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In the olfactory bulb, the brain's first relay for smell, sensory axons meet the dendrites of mitral and tufted cells in set patterns. How those dendrites grow out was less well regulated in the literature than axon targeting.

The team found the olfactory epithelium, the smell-sensing sheet in the nose, influences that outgrowth. Its signals shape how mitral and tufted cell dendrites develop. The result shows the sensory surface talking back to the brain wiring it feeds.
plos-pone-0003916:
João Fadista, Marianne Nygaard, Lars-Erik Holm, and co-authors gave a first survey of pig genome variation in 2008. Recent work showed mammal genomes vary in how many copies of regions they carry. Those copy number variants help shape traits, health, and disease. Pigs had not yet had such a survey.

Their PLOS ONE article reports variants across parts of chromosomes 4, 7, 14, and 17. It offers a first snapshot rather than a whole-genome count. Pig breeders and researchers can build on that start. The data also aid use of pigs as models for human disease.
plos-pone-0004016:
Robert M. Suryan, David J. Anderson, Scott A. Shaffer, and co-authors linked albatross form to their ranges in 2008. Large albatrosses harvest wind and wave energy for cheap long flights. Their wing shape suits the windy oceans they patrol. Most species therefore stay in those wind belts.

Their PLOS ONE article argues that specialization may limit range expansion. Endangered albatrosses cannot easily shift as oceans warm. Wings built for strong winds perform poorly in calm zones. Conservation plans must account for that built-in limit on movement. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004116:
Marie-Christine Meunier, Chantal Baron, and Claude Perreault tracked cancer-fighting T cells in mice in 2009. CD8 T cells primed against minor antigens can erase leukemia and solid tumors. The H7a antigen is one such target in their model. Why these cells work so potently was not fully clear.

Their PLOS ONE article follows the injected cells inside tumor-bearing mice. Two host factors governed how long the T cells persisted. Persistence likely decides whether tumors return after early success. Knowing the factors could improve cell therapy design. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004216:
Mary Anna Carbone and colleagues published this glaucoma study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Glaucoma is the world's second leading cause of bilateral blindness, killing retinal ganglion cells over time. The protein myocilin is tied to congenital glaucoma. It is also tied to two to four percent of primary open angle glaucoma cases. But how it causes disease was unclear.

The team overproduced myocilin in the fruit fly eye. They report that this activates the unfolded protein response, the cell's alarm for misfolded proteins. The result points to protein-folding stress as the route from myocilin to eye damage.
plos-pone-0004316:
Michael Seidman and colleagues published this inflammation genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Knocking out or inhibiting PECAM, an adhesion molecule on blood vessel walls, impairs inflammatory responses in several mouse strains. Yet on the C57BL/6 background, no such phenotype appears, hinting that other genes compensate.

The team studied thioglycollate peritonitis, a standard belly inflammation model, in these mice. They report a PECAM-independent form of the response associated with a locus on mouse chromosome 2. A backup inflammation route, mapped to one chromosome region, may explain why the knockout disappoints. The locus is a stretch of DNA whose exact gene is still to be named.
plos-pone-0004416: In 2009, a German team found human skin cells stockpiling an enzyme. Skin cells stored glutamine synthetase by age and body site studied. The skin's chemical pantry varied widely. The map informs skin science today. The enzyme aids growth and detox work.
plos-pone-0004516: In 2009, Schwartz, Oren, and Bester found fragile DNA in immune patients. Cells from immunodeficiency patients with Cernunnos/XLF mutations showed impaired replication stress response. The repair defect left DNA fragile. The finding links repair to immunity. The gene serves NHEJ repair.
plos-pone-0004616: In 2009, Teacher, Garner, and Nichols found selection shaping a frog immune gene. Evidence for directional selection at a novel MHC class I marker in wild amphibians was found. The immune marker evolved fast. The finding maps wildlife immunity. The marker is novel.
plos-pone-0004716: In 2009, a team found a bug signal receptor sparking egg release anew here today. The OAMB receptor drove egg release onward. The receptor worked through a calcium signal anew. The study maps insect body wiring. The egg process is vital indeed.
mandelstam-stone-1916:
Osip Mandelstam called his first book of poems Stone, and the second Russian edition of 1916 gathers his early work. He wrote of buildings, music, and the old Greek and Roman world. Each poem is built with care, like a wall of cut stone.

Young Mandelstam rejected vague mystic moods in favor of clear, solid images. Cathedrals, domes, and ancient myths carry weight and order in his verse. The book announced a poet of rare skill and learning. Later readers would rank him among the finest Russian poets of the twentieth century, and Stone shows why.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-16:
Huronia in 1639 stands at its high point in Volume 16, from 1898. Sainte-Marie among the Hurons rises as a walled mission headquarters. Thwaites prints the reports of a work that seems to have arrived.

Sainte-Marie was the most bold building project in New France then. Stores, chapels, and safe walls serve priests, workers, and guests. The fathers write like men who trust the future is theirs. Yet success and death march toward them hand in hand. Readers who know the end feel the height before the fall. Pride in the work rings through each letter home.
journal-of-discourses-vol-16:
Volume Sixteen, from 1874, was preached as the legal noose tightened. Marshals raid homes while church leaders dodge arrest across Utah. The anti-polygamy drive turns from threat into daily, grinding fact.

Young's voice stays steady as the pressure mounts on his people. Sermons teach patience, secrecy where needed, and unbroken faith in God. Families learn to live with prison hanging over their fathers' heads. Faith practiced under the law's shadow fills these hard, brave pages. The Saints' resolve is tested here and, by their account, holds firm against the storm. Ordinary families, not just leaders, carry the volume's quiet heroism.
commons-principles-labor-legislation-191:
Commons and John Andrews published Principles of Labor Legislation in 1916, a handbook for the reform movement. Both men worked at the center of the campaign for better labor law in the Progressive Era. The book argues the case for public rules on work, state by state and topic by topic.

Chapters take up hours of labor, workplace safety, child labor, and the new idea of social insurance against sickness, accidents, and old age. The authors compare the laws of American states with those of Europe and judge what works. Their manual gave legislators and activists a shared program and a shared evidence base. Much of the labor law of the next generation, state and federal, grew from the agenda set out in these pages.
cia-0000009716:
Low Pathet Lao morale, the local economy, propaganda work, and prison matters share one wide CIA paper from October 1971. The heading shortens the Pathet Lao to PL and stacks four subjects in a single report. Such bundles often came from one source's broad debriefing in Laos.

Mixed reports show intelligence gathering as it really happened: whatever a source knew, taken down together. Morale and food prices could matter as much as prison news for judging the enemy's strength. Analysts sorted the bundle into files afterward. This entry preserves the bundle whole, a snapshot of everyday reporting from the secret war.
cia-0000009916:
Four American pilots were held at a cave at Hang Long, east of Sam Neua in Houa Phan province, an October 1967 item states. Hang Long's caves lie in the same limestone belt as the Pathet Lao's wartime cave capital. Four men in one cave made a sizable group for Laos.

A group in a fixed cave could be watched, in principle, far better than men in shifting camps. In practice, the cave country stayed closed to outsiders for years. The report at least fixed the men's place in the autumn of 1967. Later files on Sam Neua prisoners build on points like this.
cia-0000012416:
September 30, 1961: meeting number thirty-six closes the month's intensive Paris run. The month's debriefings had been relentless by any standard. Session followed session through the early autumn, and the handlers' notebooks filled accordingly. Their source stayed willing, his memory stayed exact, and the questions stayed ahead of the answers by design.

The record tallies September in the series' plain numbering. It closes a month that proved Paris could carry the case as London had. For readers, the page marks a season's end inside an operation that still had no way to know its own.
cia-0000013616:
Uruguay's growing troubles fill a CIA paper from May 1965 on the situation there. The small republic had long been South America's calm exception: prosperous, democratic, and dull in the best sense. By 1965 the old calm was fraying. Prices rose, strikes spread, and a city guerrilla movement, the Tupamaros, was just beginning to stir in the capital's streets.

The paper senses the turn early. It weighs the economy, the parties, and the first signs of armed revolt together. For readers, it keeps the watch on a model republic at the moment its luck began to run out.
cia-0000013916: How North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces treated American and South Vietnamese captives fills a CIA report dated November 5, 1967. The report spans both the northern army and the southern Viet Cong. It also spans both sets of prisoners, U.S. and Saigon government men. Broad treatment reports like this set the base line for judging single camp claims.
cia-0000015316: A letter to Lawrence Tacker from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated May 3, 1958. Strong enclosed the letter the office had received, per the title. Routing a writer's own letter back with a fresh cover was a standard move. The file keeps the paper loop of the saucer debate turning one more time.
cia-0000015416: Major Donald E. Keyhoe, the best-known saucer writer of his day, sent an inquiry that the CIA logged on January 4, 1959. Part of the record was cut before release. Keyhoe led a civilian group that pressed the government for candor on flying objects. His questions forced officials to answer in writing, and those exchanges fill many files from the late nineteen fifties.
cia-0000020316: Two bullets tied to the killing of Castillo Armas were definitely the same caliber, an untitled CIA record dated in 1957 notes. Carlos Castillo Armas was president of Guatemala when he was shot that year. A caliber match is a small hard fact in a case full of rumor. The note shows field reporting carrying forensic detail back to headquarters.
cia-0000022316: Gary Powers' trial would be public, and American policy was on trial too, a CIA record dated in 1960 argues in its heading. Moscow staged the August 1960 trial before the world press. Powers faced espionage charges after his U-2 fell in Soviet land. The heading's claim rang true for many watchers, since Washington's spy flights stood judged beside the pilot.
cia-0000044016:
Rosa Chavez commented on the Jesuits' killing, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. Chavez spoke from inside El Salvador's church community. Church workers lived close to the war's daily violence and loss.

Inside, her comments on the murders are preserved as she gave them. A voice like hers carried the grief of a working parish. It lacked the polish of a president's statement, and gained force from that. The file holds one woman's witness beside the generals and ministers, and hers may be the voice that best shows what the killings meant at ground level.
cia-0000044116: An unidentified flying object report survives in a CIA record dated November 2, 1968, with the title noting that the publication date is estimated. Saucer reports reached the agency in large numbers during the 1950s and 1960s, and each one was logged in the same plain way. This record's own dating is part of its interest, since even the file could not fix when its report first appeared. It stands as a routine page from the long official file on things seen in the sky and never explained.
cia-0000045216:
A bishop predicted a wave of reprisals, in a CIA record dated September 6, 1985. Reprisals were the war's habit: each blow answered by another. A bishop's warning carried the voice of the church into the crisis.

Inside, the forecast of revenge attacks is preserved as he made it. Warnings from the pulpit reached people no communique could reach. They also named the cycle that kept the war feeding itself. The file holds the prediction from that September, spoken by a churchman who had watched reprisal follow reprisal for years and saw no reason it would stop.
cia-0000049016: A CIA item from 1981 traces responsibility for a death squad run by businessman Ricardo Sol Mesa in El Salvador. Private money behind public murder was one of the war's worst features, and this item names a funder. It survives in the Truth Commission files, where the money trails mattered as much as the trigger men.
cia-0000049216: A partly blacked-out file on Colonel Jose Chavez Caceres survives in a CIA item from 1992, kept with the Truth Commission records. By 1992 the peace accords had ended the war, and files on its officers passed to history's keeping. What the redactions still guard sits inside the document, for the next reader.
cia-0000096716: Prominent author Pa Chin singled out for struggle by a Shanghai rebel faction is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000096716, dated June 3, 1968. The heading names the writer and the faction's act. The brief file records a cultural figure targeted in Shanghai, preserved as a short item on the human cost of factional campaigns.

plos-pone-0004816: Obesity is rising in Pakistan's youth, but hard numbers were scarce. Warraich and colleagues surveyed schoolchildren in Karachi for obesity and malnutrition prevalence. The cross-sectional data reveal a double burden. Public health's youngest front line, measured classroom by classroom across Karachi.
plos-pone-0005416: Prisons concentrate HIV risk, but in-prison transmission is poorly documented. Jafa and team investigated 88 HIV seroconversions among Georgia male inmates from 1988 to 2005. The disease tracking informs prevention policy. Tracing the virus behind bars across seventeen years of Georgia prison records.
plos-pone-0005516: Nerves and fat talk to each other, but the conversation is poorly mapped. Ruschke and colleagues linked defective peripheral nerves to abnormal fat architecture in Nscl-2 mutant mice. The neuro-adipose axis shapes metabolism. When nerves fail, fat follows suit metabolically.
plos-pone-0005616: Female cells silence one X DNA bundle randomly, but what sets the odds? Monkhorst and team showed the X-to-autosome ratio and allelic properties determine inactivation probability. The stochastic process has rules. Chance with a formula, in mammalian cells, genes of dosage make-up.
plos-pone-0005716: Plant cell motion need number-based imaging. Elgass and team combined fluorescence lifetime and microscopy for subcellular motion in plant cells. The methods enable predictive plant biology. Watching plant cells in number-based detail, lifetime by lifetime, living physics serving botany, with subcellular resolution and number-based output.
plos-pone-0005816: Fish breeding follows season rhythms. Zhang and team defined neuroendocrine gene patterns of breeding seasons in fish. The goldfish model shows HPG-axis control. plos-pone-0006416: Gene data needs slim pickers. Gutkin and team built SlimPLS to pick key genes for disease sorting. The lean method beats bloat — choosing genes wisely, for doctors, with cases versus controls. Big gene lists tamed, sorter training eased: med sorting improved.
plos-pone-0006516: A floppy protein part gets its shape mapped. Chen modeled the phosphorylated KID domain's moves. The tag orders the floppy bit — protein origami, computed, in silico, with NMR hints. Shapeless alone, with a KIX partner: gene switch role, moves run.
plos-pone-0006616: Bax drives two-speed eye decay. Hamann and team found Bax-driven cell death kills rods slowly, cones fast in LCA mice. The dual role, mapped — blindness' two clocks, mapped, in Rpe65 knockout. Null background, creeping loss: early cone death, disease path charted.
plos-pone-0009416: Stroke a hidden real hand while someone watches a rubber one, and the brain starts feeling touch in the fake hand — but how far can the trick go? Volunteers were asked about impossible touches, like feeling a tap from a ghostly or divine source on a non-hand object. The study maps the outer limits of body illusion, showing even spooky explanations can't stop the brain from claiming a strange object as its own.
plos-pone-0009516: When the cell's protein factory is overwhelmed, it first tries to cope — then orders the cell to die. This study shows the protein C/EBP-beta controls that fatal decision in mouse and human cells under ER stress. The paper identifies a master switch in the cell's suicide program, with relevance to diseases from diabetes to neurodegeneration.
plos-pone-0009616: Cells balance growth and self-destruction through the Hippo pathway, where the kinase MST2 promotes cell death. This study shows the IGF1-Akt growth pathway restrains MST2. The paper maps a tug-of-war between living and dying — a balance whose failure feeds cancer.
plos-pone-0010416: Jared Diamond argued geography shaped human civilization — but how far does that go? This study tests whether climate and soil alone explain the distribution of basic economic traits across societies. The paper puts a famous big-history thesis to a statistical test.
plos-pone-0010516: Classifying land cover from satellites needs reliable spectral fingerprints. This study tests whether signatures generalized across images improve accuracy.
