plos-pone-0010616: Some fish change sex — and males and females end up different sizes. This study compares two populations to find why dimorphism differs. The paper explores how social life shapes bodies. The comparison shows the environment sculpting sex itself in real time.
plos-pone-0010716: Great tits need carotenoids — the pigments behind bright feathers. This diet-choice study shows the birds actively seek carotenoid-rich foods in captivity and the wild. The paper documents a nutrient-specific appetite. The craving ties diet to health, color, and courtship.
plos-pone-0010816: Cuckoos lay eggs that mimic their hosts' — and hosts fight back. This study documents disruptive selection on egg color in a brood parasite and its host. The paper captures an evolutionary arms race. The duel pushes both sides toward extreme egg phenotypes.
plos-pone-0010916: Oxygen-starved newborn brains need protection. This rat study shows inhaled nitric oxide blunts excitotoxic brain damage in neonates. The paper tests a gentle therapy. The gas could safeguard vulnerable infants. The breathable drug shields developing newborn minds from injury.
plos-pone-0011016: Stroke kills brain cells — but the brain tries to rebuild. This rat study shows erythropoietin amplifies the birth of new oligodendrocytes after stroke. The paper reveals a hormone-driven repair boost. The finding suggests EPO as a stroke-recovery aid. The boost could limit lasting disability.
plos-pone-0011116: Gecko ears produce faint sounds all by themselves. This computational study shows interactions between hair cells shape spontaneous otoacoustic emissions in a tokay gecko cochlea model. The paper reveals auditory self-organization. The finding informs hearing research. The self-organization tunes the inner ear.
plos-pone-0011216: A vaccine's shape steers the immune response. This study shows straight versus branched fat-sugar peptide vaccines take different immune pathways and spark different tumor killing. The paper reveals a design rule. The finding aids cancer shots. The rule optimizes vaccine blueprints.
plos-pone-0011316: A repurposed drug helps transplanted blood stem cells settle in. This mouse study shows the CXCR4 antagonist AMD3100 selectively enhances donor hematopoietic cell engraftment. The paper offers a transplant boost. The finding informs bone marrow transplantation. The informed transplants succeed more often.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1216:
The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 23 July 1945. A message from the commander in chief to an envoy carried orders and backing that no office could supply. It reached China from the middle of the Potsdam talks.

Hurley's mission was among the hardest in the service: hold a divided China to the allied cause. Word from the president himself steadied that mission and set its line. This note is the top of the American state speaking to its man in Chungking. It shows the summit's leader tending a distant front of the same war, by cable, between sessions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1316:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Collado, who directed the office of financial and development policy, on 16 July 1945. The note went out the day before the summit opened. It joined the department's chief-in-waiting to its top money-planning desk.

Collado's office shaped how American funds would rebuild trade and growth after the war. Guidance to it on the summit's eve aligned that planning with the talks to come. This message is one piece of the department's money machinery starting its Potsdam work. It shows the peace being budgeted before it was signed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1416:
The Protocol of the Proceedings of the Yalta Conference is reprinted near the end of the Potsdam volume. Yalta, in February 1945, was the earlier summit where Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin set much of the frame that Potsdam later filled in. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Printing the Yalta protocol here lets readers compare the two settlements side by side. Promises made in the Crimea about Poland, Germany, and the United Nations were tested at Potsdam five months later. The protocol lists the earlier choices in the leaders' own agreed words. Anyone tracing how wartime accord slid toward cold war will want the two texts open together, which is just what the editors arranged.
frus-1945-50-intel-d16:
Stone of the Budget Bureau wrote to Director Harold Smith again on 20 September 1945. That was the day the president's order ended the OSS and split its duties between two departments. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff papers written on the day of a big decision usually handle the follow-through: who moves, who pays, who signs what next. Stone's memorandum belongs to that practical layer of history. Readers who want to know how a famous order becomes real desks and budgets will find the Budget Bureau's same-day papers instructive. The bureau's men thought in terms of execution, and their memos show the machinery catching up with the president's pen.
frus-1945-50-intel-d116:
Hoover wrote to Braden, assistant secretary for American republic affairs, on 22 July 1946. The FBI director carried his Latin American case to the State Department's own regional chief. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Writing to Braden was a flanking move: if the policy bureau that owned Latin America backed the FBI's work there, the CIG's claim would weaken. Hoover rarely missed such a step. Readers can see the bureau's defense in depth here, allies cultivated in the departments while the chiefs exchanged letters above. Braden's own February paper to Byrnes, printed earlier in the volume, shows why Hoover chose him. The regional chief had already shown he cared who collected intelligence in his hemisphere.
frus-1945-50-intel-d216:
A memorandum dated 29 May 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative LiaisonDivision, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It stands as document 216 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d316:
Dated 21 June 1950, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner) to Mr. Miller of His Staff. It stands as document 316 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d416:
Roscoe Hillenkoetter, the Director of Central Intelligence, wrote to Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson on 17 February 1950. The letter is document 416 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Defense Department held most of the money and staff in American intelligence. Its secretary dealt with the CIA as both a partner and a rival. A formal letter from the agency's chief to the Pentagon's head shows the care with which the two sides handled each other. Johnson's Pentagon and Acheson's State Department feuded in public that year, which makes formal letters between their chiefs read with extra care.
frus-1861-d16:
To his minister in Prussia, Norman Judd, William H. Seward wrote on 12 August 1861. The letter is document 16 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By August the war had settled into a long struggle, and Seward's tone abroad grew firm. He wanted no foreign court to mistake Union resolve. A mid summer letter to Berlin kept Prussia inside the circle of governments held to strict neutrality by steady pressure. Prussia stayed correct and cool all year, in part through this steady stream of letters. Cool correctness from Berlin was a gain the South felt as a quiet loss.
frus-1861-d116:
On 12 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Jones, closing a summer of reports. The letter is document 116 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's August note answers the line of reports Jones had sent that summer. The record heading names no post for Jones, which keeps the focus on the exchange itself. It shows the Secretary closing a loop with one of his far flung reporters. Answers from Seward often took weeks to reach his posts, which made each one count. Each answer that counted had to be right the first time it was penned.
frus-1861-d216:
6 July 1861 is the date on a dispatch from Mr. Marsh to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 216 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d16:
10 February 1862 brought Charles Francis Adams a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 16 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d116:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 1 August 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 116 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d216:
F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State. He wrote to Lord Lyons on 14 June 1862, in a note printed as Document 216 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Frederick William Seward was the Secretary's son and his second at the Department.

Notes signed by the assistant usually mean the Secretary was away, ill, or letting a matter move at a lower level. The Lyons channel could not pause for one man's calendar, since British business arrived daily. This brief note shows the Department's work passing smoothly between father and son in the middle of a demanding summer. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d316:
The third Seward dispatch of 24 September 1862 stands as Document 316 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like the others, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris.

Late September's great question in Paris was whether France would press its truce plan. Emancipation had just raised the political price of aiding the South. Dayton needed current instructions and current facts. This letter, one of four that day, helped supply both, and it shows how much paper a turning point could generate. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d416:
Horace J. Perry reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Madrid on 15 March 1862, a week after his previous dispatch. The letter is Document 416 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reports were the rhythm of a working legation. From Madrid, Perry covered Spanish politics, the Mexican expedition, and the treatment of American trade and ships. In March 1862 Union arms were advancing in the West, and news of victory helped the Union case at every court. Reports like this one told Seward what Madrid believed about the war, so he could answer error and rumor before they hardened into policy.
frus-1862-d516:
James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 September 1862. It is Document 516 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

September opened with Lee crossing into Maryland. Pike, though, could only write of what The Hague knew. That was rumor, old news, and the Dutch ministry's steady reserve. His report added the Netherlands to the list of courts watching the autumn campaign before deciding anything. Seward valued such reports because they told him where no action was needed, which in 1862 was valuable knowledge. The letter is part of the early-September Hague file, written in the held breath before Antietam.
frus-1862-d616:
On 8 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister to Denmark. The instruction is Document 616 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward wrote two days after Shiloh, in the season when his orders abroad mixed battle news with standing business. With Denmark the standing business was the law and practice of trade and shipping between two friendly states. Copenhagen's court was absorbed in the Schleswig-Holstein tangle with the German powers. It had attention to spare for America mainly in two roles. America was a customer and a fellow maritime state. The dispatch keeps the Danish file's even temper, a small northern thread in a volume of hotter correspondence.
frus-1862-d716:
William H. Seward sent this reply to Luis Molina on 1 October 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington, and the two men had traded letters all through the fall. The letter is document 716 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Seward's side of such an exchange mixed courtesy with the hard edge of his government's aims. His letters to Molina kept the Costa Rica file moving while the war news crowded his desk. For a reader, the pair of runs shows foreign business done face to face in the capital. Molina wrote in; Seward wrote back. That was a change from the ship-borne mail of the legations.
frus-1863p1-d16:
On 10 December 1862, Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed volume sets it after a letter of 18 December, out of strict date order. It is document 16 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams's December mail covered the ground a minister was meant to cover. It held talks with British officials, the temper of the press, and word on Southern agents. This letter is one of those reports. Its place out of line is a quirk of the printing, not of the work. In the run of the file it reads as part of the legation's steady December watch.
frus-1863p1-d116:
Mid-March brought this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams in London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 13 March 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 116 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-March mail from the legation kept up the spring watch on Britain. Adams reported the drift of the cabinet and the press as the ship question in British yards grew hot. His sheets were Washington's best gauge of whether Britain would act or hold back. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, in the post's usual split of its business.
frus-1863p1-d216:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 18 June 1863. The letter is document 216 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d316:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 6 November 1862. The note is document 316 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Seward answered the legation knowing London would read every word. Even routine notes carried weight, because each answer set a precedent for the next dispute. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d416:
On 16 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 416 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

British ships stopped by the Union blockade, and British subjects held as prisoners, supplied much of London's complaint list. Lyons delivered those protests in formal notes like this one. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d516:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 15 May 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d616:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 19 August 1863 letter from F. W. Seward to William Stuart. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, and Stuart held the British legation in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020416:
Daniel Ortiz-Barrientos, Brian A. Counterman, and Mohamed A. F. Noor reviewed how new species can arise in PLOS Biology in 2004. Reinforcement is the idea that natural selection strengthens barriers between two groups when their hybrid offspring are unfit. Mating with the wrong group wastes effort, so traits that prevent it spread.

The review weighs genetic evidence for the process in nature. It sorts systems where reinforcement looks real from those where other causes fit better. The question is a live one in evolution, since it bears on how species stay distinct while living side by side. A clear-eyed summary like this one helps field workers design tests that can actually settle it.
plos-pone-0000116:
Zhong Hua, Qing Lv, Wenbin Ye, and colleagues published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It examines how tiny RNA molecules called microRNAs control VEGF and other angiogenic factors. These factors drive angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, when oxygen runs low, a state called hypoxia.

Blood vessel growth feeds healing tissue, but it also feeds tumors. The authors trace how microRNAs adjust the levels of these vessel-promoting factors under low oxygen. The findings matter for cancer and eye disease research, where blocking or boosting this pathway could change how a disease progresses.
plos-pone-0000216:
Ning Fu, Ines Drinnenberg, and Janet Kelso published this comparative genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It compares humans and chimpanzees, asking how the evolution of proteins lines up with the evolution of the RNA messages that encode them. The authors measure both kinds of change across the two species.

Proteins and their messages do not always evolve at the same pace, and the mismatch is informative. The comparison shows where regulation, rather than protein change, drove differences between the species. That distinction matters for the long debate over what, genetically, makes humans different from our closest relatives.
plos-pone-0000316:
Màté A. Demény, Evi Soutoglou, Zita Nagy, and colleagues published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. TAFs are parts of the machinery that starts transcription, the reading of genes. The authors identify a small TAF complex and describe its role in assembling the larger TAF-containing complexes that switch genes on.

Gene activation is built from modular parts that snap together in steps. A small sub-complex acting as an assembly piece clarifies that construction. The work refines the parts list of the transcription machinery, one of the most fundamental systems in the cell.
plos-pone-0000416:
Shih-Chieh Hung and colleagues tested whether a brief spell of low oxygen primes healing cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The cells are multipotent stromal cells, versatile cells from marrow that can settle into damaged tissue. After short exposure to low oxygen, the team measured two surface receptors, CX3CR1 and CXCR4, and how well the cells engrafted in living tissue.

The authors report that low oxygen raised both receptors and improved engraftment in vivo. Receptors like these act as homing gear, helping cells find and enter injured sites. A simple preconditioning step that boosts homing could make cell therapies work better without genetic tinkering.
plos-pone-0000516:
Robert J. Greenstein and colleagues revisited two old drugs' action on a stubborn bacterium, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The drugs are 5-amino-salicylic acid and its partner sulfapyridine, used for bowel inflammation. The target is M. avium including subspecies paratuberculosis, a slow-growing bacterium linked to Johne's disease in cattle and debated in Crohn's disease.

Whether these drugs act directly on the bacterium matters for how they help patients. It also matters for a contested claim. That claim holds that the bacterium drives some Crohn's cases. Laboratory action studies cannot settle the disease debate, but they clarify what the drugs do to the organism itself. The paper adds data to a long argument.
plos-pone-0000616:
Jan R.T. van Weering, Ruud F. Toonen and Matthijs Verhage wrote for PLOS ONE in 2007 about the final steps before a cell releases its cargo. Rab3a is a small protein that sits on secretory vesicles, the tiny sacs that carry chemicals out of the cell. It flips between an active form bound to GTP and an inactive form bound to GDP.

Docking, the vesicle's arrival and holding at the cell surface, is the step under study. The authors tested different Rab3a forms and gene combinations, drawing on yeast work where related genes interact. Their title states that docking needs Rab3a to bind and release its phosphate partners, plus the protein Munc18-1.
plos-pone-0000716:
John P. Grieco, Nicole L. Achee, Theeraphap Chareonviriyaphap and co-authors proposed a new way to sort the chemicals sprayed on walls against malaria mosquitoes. The method is called indoor residual spraying, or IRS. How mosquitoes respond to these chemicals is of great importance. It decides how well a spray blocks the spread of malaria.

A set of lab tests measured mosquito responses in hard numbers. Some chemicals kill on contact. Others drive mosquitoes away, or merely irritate them into leaving. The authors argue these actions should be classed apart, not lumped under one label. A clear scheme helps malaria programs pick the right product, and helps scientists compare studies that long used loose terms.
plos-pone-0000816:
Adrienne C. M. Persoon, Pieter L. Jager, Wim J. Sluiter and co-authors compared two ways to watch for the return of thyroid cancer. After treatment for this cancer, doctors track a protein called thyroglobulin, or Tg, in the blood. A rise can mean the cancer is back. A very sensitive Tg test can catch small rises. So can a test done after a dose of rhTSH, a lab-made hormone that pushes Tg up.

The team weighed the yield of both tests in long-term follow-up care. The hormone route means extra shots, cost, and side effects for the patient. If the sensitive test alone does as well, patients can skip all that. Head-to-head data like this give doctors a firm base for a choice they face at every check-up.
plos-pone-0000916:
Agnes Roure, Ute Rothbacher, Francois Robin and co-authors assembled a set of gateway vectors for embryo research, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genomic data, full length gene copies and control sequences have piled up for more and more species. Comparing protein function across species needs tools that move genes between test systems with little fuss.

Their multicassette vector set is built for high throughput work in Ciona, a small sea animal, and in vertebrate embryos. A shared toolkit lets researchers run the same gene in different embryos and compare fairly. That kind of comparison is how shared developmental rules get separated from species specific twists.
plos-pone-0001016:
Roland Meier, Annick Muhlethaler-Mottet, Marjorie Flahaut and colleagues studied a receptor that fuels neuroblastoma growth, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer that varies widely and turns deadly in its higher stages. It tends to spread to the liver and bone marrow, and beyond surgery there was still no efficient treatment.

The receptor CXCR4, the team report, strongly promotes both the main tumor's growth and its spread. It did not, however, drive invasion in the same way. Splitting growth from invasion matters for drug aims: blocking one may not block the other. The receptor remains a clear target candidate.
plos-pone-0001116:
For many people with nerve damage, a light touch on the skin hurts. Loïs Miraucourt, Radhouane Dallel, and Daniel Voisin studied this symptom, called tactile allodynia, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on glycine, a chemical that normally calms signals in the spinal cord.

Their work links the pain to a failure of that calming system. When glycine-based inhibition breaks down, touch signals reach a set of spinal cord cells known as PKCgamma interneurons and get read as pain. Pinpointing this route matters because allodynia is common, hard to treat, and lacks good therapies.
plos-pone-0001216:
The season in which a person is born has been linked to traits such as novelty seeking and sensation seeking. Dan Eisenberg and colleagues tested whether that link runs through dopamine genes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Similar traits have also been linked with variants in dopamine receptor genes, which help the brain respond to the reward chemical dopamine.

The authors looked at season of birth and dopamine receptor gene links together, against impulsivity, sensation seeking, and reproductive behaviors. The two may combine, each shifting the other's effect. The study sits at the junction of environment, genes, and personality.
plos-pone-0001316:
Candida albicans is a fungus that lives on human surfaces without harm but can cause inflammation when it turns pathogenic. Eric Haas-Stapleton and colleagues report a striking ability of this fungus in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Resolvins are anti-inflammatory lipids, derived from omega-3 fatty acids, that help calm neutrophil-driven inflammation.

The authors show that Candida albicans modulates host defense by biosynthesizing the pro-resolving mediator resolvin E1. This fungus making the body's own peace signal could dampen the attack against it. The finding changes how this common fungus is thought to work with immunity.
plos-pone-0001416:
Rico Tabor and Rainer Friedrich wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on smell circuits in the zebrafish brain. Receptors that sense the amino acid glutamate shape how smell signals are handled. Their roles had been studied in dishes, but not in the whole intact brain. The pair used drugs to probe these receptors during odor handling.

By blocking or boosting each receptor type, they mapped which ones sharpen or blur the smell pattern. The maps show how local circuits sort odors before they reach higher brain areas. That sorting is a core step in how animals tell one scent from the next. The work grounds circuit theory in a living, smelling brain.
plos-pone-0001516:
Stijn De Langhe and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on lung growth and a key signal. The signal, run through a protein called beta catenin, helps form many body lineages. Its role in lung tissue lineages was vague. The team switched the signal off in the early lung tissue of mouse embryos.

Loss of the signal threw the forming of lung cell types off course. More than one lineage was hit at once. That breadth shows the signal acts as a master switch in the young lung. The work helps frame birth defects of the lung and may guide lung repair studies.
plos-pone-0001616:
Jyothi Mallajosyula and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme and Parkinson's disease. Levels of this enzyme, MAO-B, rise in the brain with age. That rise may add to the nerve loss of Parkinson's. A drug that blocks it is a long used therapy, paired with the standard dopamine drug. The team raised the enzyme in mouse brain support cells.

Mice with more of the enzyme in those cells grew Parkinson's like harm. That is direct proof the rise is not a mere side mark of age. It firms the case for blocker drugs. It also flags support cells as actors in the disease, not just stage hands.
plos-pone-0001716:
Carmelo Mario Vicario, Patrizia Pecoraro, Patrizia Turriziani, and their co-authors tested how space warps felt time in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Time, space, and numbers are linked in the physical world and, it seems, in the mind. The authors borrowed a relativity metaphor: just as motion bends time in physics, position and size may bend duration judgments in perception.

They asked whether judging how long digits stayed on screen is biased by where the digits appeared, left or right, and by their magnitude. The full text gives the timing tasks and the bias patterns. Such biases show that the brain's clock is not a neutral stopwatch. That point matters for models of timing and for tests used in brain disorders.
plos-pone-0001816:
Chad J. Creighton analyzed gene activity patterns in prostate tumors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gene transcription patterns linked to activation of oncogenes had been generated in experimental models. The oncogenes include Myc, c-Src, beta-catenin, E2F3, H-Ras, and HER2, and patterns also covered the cell cycle and androgen signaling.

Creighton asked whether these pathway signatures show coordinate expression patterns in human prostate tumors: whether pathways turn on together in real patients. The full text gives the tumor data sets and the signature correlations. Coordinated pathways suggest combination drug strategies, since blocking one route may leave its partners still driving the tumor.
plos-pone-0001916:
Gerard van der Krogt and co-authors fine-tuned a glowing sensor for a key cell signal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The sensor tracks cAMP, a messenger inside cells, and glows in a way that shifts with cAMP level. It is built from a protein called Epac joined to two glowing tags, one that gives light and one that takes it.

The method, called FRET, reads the shift in glow as a live measure. The team compared pairs of glowing tags to find the pair that gives the clearest signal. A better sensor lets labs watch signals rise and fall in real time inside living cells.
plos-pone-0002016:
Satyaprakash Nayak and co-authors tested a theory of robust design against cancer data, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Living systems are robust: they keep working when conditions shift. The flip side, fragility, means a small nudge can cause total failure. A theory called highly optimized tolerance says systems tuned hard for one setting hide such fragile points.

The team tested that theory on the cell cycle, the steps by which cells divide. They report that fragile cell-cycle steps match the targets hit in clinical cancer trials. If fragility maps to drug targets, the theory could help pick the next targets on purpose.
plos-pone-0002116:
Jerome Casas, Thomas Steinmann, and Olivier Dangles measured the air stirred up by running spiders, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many predators hunt in two modes: lying in ambush, or cruising in search of prey. Those modes have classically been studied for their energy costs, mechanics, and ecology, without weighing the signals a predator gives off and prey can perceive.

Wolf spiders run as they hunt, and their motion pushes air in a pattern prey hairs can feel. The team charted that aerodynamic signature. If prey can read the airflow, a running hunter betrays itself, and stealth becomes part of the hunting equation.
plos-pone-0002216:
Dominique Berrebi and co-authors searched for markers that flag the most dangerous kidney tumors of childhood, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nephroblastoma, also called Wilms tumor, varies widely: some cases stay local while others spread far. Cell cycle markers offered a possible way to tell them apart in advance.

The team measured cyclin E, a protein that pushes cells through division, and Ki-67, a marker of cell growth, in tumor samples. High cyclin E staining in tumor cells tracked with more aggressive disease. A marker like this could help doctors pick which children need stronger treatment from the start.
plos-pone-0002316:
Anna Linderholm, Helena Malmström, Kerstin Lidén, and co-authors warned about hidden contamination in ancient DNA samples, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ancient human DNA has been handled cautiously since problems with it surfaced in the early 1990s. Yet sequence data from old specimens underpin many studies of evolution and past ecology, so interest keeps growing.

The authors describe cryptic contamination, modern DNA that slips in without obvious signs. It can quietly lead to phylogenetic nonsense, family trees built on false sequences. Their cautions help labs tell genuine ancient results from artifacts, a basic hygiene issue for a field that reads history from bones.
plos-pone-0002416:
Led by Rappoport, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Joshua Z. Rappoport, Katherine P. Heyman, Shahrnaz Kemal, and others. Its subject is dynamics of Dynamin during Clathrin Mediated Endocytosis in PC12 Cells. Members of the dynamin super-family of GTPases are involved in disparate cellular pathways.

Dynamin1 and dynamin2 have been implicated in clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002516:
Research by Ancuta and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Petronela Ancuta, Anupa Kamat, Kevin J. Kunstman, and others. Its subject is microbial Translocation Is Associated with Increased Monocyte Activation and Dementia in AIDS Patients. Elevated plasma lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an indicator of microbial translocation from the gut, is a likely cause of systemic immune activation in chronic HIV infection.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002616:
Graham and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Laurie A. Graham, Stephen C. Lougheed, K. Vanya Ewart, and others. Its subject is lateral Transfer of a Lectin-Like Antifreeze Protein Gene in Fishes.

The scattered distribution of five highly diverse AFP types across phylogenetically disparate fish species is puzzling. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002716:
Work by Joshua K. Hartshorne and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with visual working memory capacity and proactive interference. The catalog record names Joshua K. Hartshorne first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Visual working memory capacity is extremely limited and appears to be relatively immune to practice effects or the use of explicit strategies. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002816:
Work by Christine F. Skibola and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was polymorphisms in the estrogen receptor 1 and vitamin c and matrix metalloproteinase gene families are associated with susceptibility to lymphoma. Authorship is credited in the record to Christine F. Skibola and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is the fifth most common cancer in the U.S. The authors add a further point. And few causes have been identified. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002916:
Elias Gounaris, Ching Tung, Clifford Restaino and colleagues imaged inflammation and polyp growth in living tissue in 2008. Up to 30 percent of polyps found in patients may shrink on their own. Judging whether a cancer therapy works needs a readout of such regression, which is hard to get.

Their method uses a light-based probe switched on by cysteine-cathepsin enzymes, which are active at sites of inflammation. Live imaging then reveals focal inflammation, new vessel growth, and polyp change over time. Published in PLOS ONE, the approach lets researchers watch disease sites respond without cutting tissue out.
plos-pone-0003016:
Qing-Peng Kong, Antonio Salas, Chang Sun and co-authors tackled fake recombinants in mitochondrial DNA datasets in 2008. Large sequencing projects handle many fragments from different genomes, creating a high risk of sample mix-ups in the lab. For genetic markers, such confusion can fabricate artificial recombinant sequences.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team offers a way to distill, or filter out, artificial recombinants from large sets of complete mitochondrial genomes. Clean data matter because mitochondrial trees underpin studies of human origins and disease. The method helps curators spot lab-made chimeras before they mislead analysis. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003116:
Else Marie Agger, Ida Rosenkrands, Jon Hansen and co-authors tested a liposome adjuvant called CAF01 in 2008. For vaccines against influenza, malaria, and HIV, antibody responses alone are not enough; a strong cell-based response is also needed for enough protection. Some diseases need still other response types, so one adjuvant rarely fits all.

CAF01 pairs cationic liposomes with a synthetic form of mycobacterial cord factor. The team presents it as a versatile adjuvant for vaccines with different immune needs. Published in PLOS ONE, such range in an adjuvant would make vaccine design simpler across diseases. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003216:
Reginia H. Y. Yan, Jessica L. Malisch, Robert M. Hannon and colleagues test a famous finger ratio claim in mice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The ratio of second digit length to fourth digit length tends to be lower in men than in women. This 2D:4D ratio is often used as a proxy for prenatal androgen exposure in studies of human health and behaviour.

By selective breeding for a behavioural trait, the team show digit ratio itself can change. Readers learn that the ratio is not a fixed fossil of hormone exposure alone. The result urges caution when finger measures are used to explain human behaviour.
plos-pone-0003316:
Zhi-Hua Chen and co-authors link a stress gene to cell cleanup in damaged lungs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. COPD is a lung disease that gets worse over time. Cigarette smoke drives odd cell responses that break down lung tissue and narrow air flow. Autophagy, where cells digest their own worn parts in lysosomes, is part of that response.

The title reports the gene Egr-1 controls autophagy in smoke-induced COPD. Readers see a stress switch tied to a cleanup path that can help or harm, in excess. Tuning that path may be one way to slow smoke damage in lungs.
plos-pone-0007416: Do chimpanzees help on purpose, or only by accident? This study tested targeted helping by giving one chimp a tool-request problem and watching whether another would hand over exactly the right tool. The chimps reliably helped — but only when asked. That distinction shows their aid is deliberate, directed at a partner's goal rather than random generosity.
plos-pone-0007516: Among orb-weaving spiders, the genus Nephila includes some of the largest web-builders on Earth. This 2009 study describes the discovery of the largest known species and asks how such giants evolved. Tracing gigantism through the group reveals the evolutionary pressures that push spiders toward enormous size.
plos-pone-0007616: The striatum helps control movement, but its exact role in walking is murky. This study lesioned one side of the striatum in rats and filmed their 3D gait, including how they stepped over obstacles. The detailed motion analysis shows the striatum fine-tunes both routine and challenged walking.
plos-pone-0007716: Fish blood vessels got a 3D nano-movie. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Armer's team caught vessel-fusion moments in zebrafish with volume electron microscopy. Living events need both space and time detail. The fusion clips were captured. The movie feeds vessel biology.
plos-pone-0007816: Prion clumps got a clean-catch trick. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Biasini's team fished pathological prion clumps out of tissue with antibodies. Misfolded prions drive fatal brain disease. The clean-catch method was validated. The trick feeds prion research.
plos-pone-0007916: Ovarian cancer hides in the complexity of blood proteins. This study combined proteomics of human cancer cells and plasma from tumor-bearing mice to hunt biomarkers. The integrated approach fishes candidates from the noise of the plasma proteome.
plos-pone-0008016: Pain is subjective, but brain imaging may objectify it. This study used diffuse optical tomography to distinguish painful from non-painful heat in the somatosensory cortex. The specific activation patterns are a step toward a pain meter.
plos-pone-0008116: Building evolutionary trees got a user-friendly overhaul. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Chen and colleagues released PALM, a software framework that picks DNA models on its own and builds trees on parallel computers. Choosing the right model by hand demands deep expertise, which shuts out many biologists. PALM's auto-pick handles that chore, and its parallel design chews through big datasets. The tool puts rigorous tree-building within reach of researchers who just want reliable answers about how species relate.
plos-pone-0008216: Bone scores were linked to how well elders function. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Berkemeyer's team tested whether bone T-scores, the osteoporosis yardstick, track functional status in German seniors. Brittle bones threaten independence. The cross-sectional snapshot tied scan numbers to daily-life ability. The link supports watching bone health as a window on aging well.
plos-pone-0008316: Spreading tumors got a glowing tracker. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Chung's team engineered tumor cells to secrete Gaussia luciferase as a beacon for metastases. Few tools can count scattered tumors in live animals. The secreted glow reports growth and treatment response in real time. The beacon enables sensitive drug tests in mice.
plos-pone-0008416: Fish muscle assembly got two chaperone suspects. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Codina's team knocked down Smyhc1 and Hsp90alpha1 one by one in zebrafish embryos and watched muscle fibers form. Both proteins help sarcomeres line up. The two knockdowns broke the build in unlike ways. The unlike outcomes split their jobs apart. The side-by-side test clarifies the muscle's construction crew.
plos-pone-0008516: A gene was linked to longshot betting. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zhong's team tied the MAOA gene to attitudes toward longshot risks. People flip between risk-loving and risk-averse on long odds. The gene variant tracked the tilt. The link adds genetics to gambling behavior.
plos-pone-0008616: Nicotine's reward hook got an NMDA link. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Wang's team showed deleting NMDA receptors in dopamine neurons blocks nicotine-conditioned place preference. The addiction circuit needed mapping. The knockout broke the hook. The link reveals addiction's wiring.
plos-pone-0008716: Immune cells' membrane nibbling got picky. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Daubeuf's team showed T and B cells preferentially snatch certain membrane proteins via trogocytosis. The selective nibbling was mapped. The pickiness reveals immune mechanics.
plos-pone-0008816: An HIV vaccine got another phase 1 trial. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Vasan's team tested ADMVA, a vaccinia-vector HIV-1 B'/C vaccine, for safety and immunogenicity. The dose escalation was run. The trial advances HIV vaccines.
plos-pone-0008916: A tumor virus got a liver-safe tune. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Leja's team tuned a tumor-killing adenovirus to stall in liver cells while killing nerve-tumor cells. The stall switch was mapped. The tune advances tumor-virus care.
plos-pone-0009016: Cord-versus-marrow stem cells got a fire-signal test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Prasanna's team set cord-jelly against marrow stem cells under fire signals. The differing immune tempers were mapped. The test feeds cell-therapy picks.
plos-pone-0009116: Worker bees' scent responses got a gene link. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kocher's team correlated individual pheromone-response variation with reproductive traits and brain gene expression in worker honey bees. The behavior-gene links were mapped. The link informs social-insect biology.
plos-pone-0009216: Strep's slime habit got a pilus rap. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Rinaudo's team showed pilus type 2a drives biofilm formation in group B streptococcus. The pilus-biofilm link was mapped. The rap informs newborn-infection control.
plos-pone-0009316: Prion protein's repeat zone got a shape-shift read. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Yam's team showed the octarepeat region is conformationally altered in PrPSc. The misfolding rearrangement was mapped. The read feeds prion science.
plos-pone-0011416: Starting HIV drugs during an opportunistic infection can trigger a dangerous flare called immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, or IRIS. This research paper analyzes risk factors for IRIS in a trial comparing early versus deferred antiretroviral therapy. Pinpointing who is most at risk helps doctors time the start of HIV treatment more safely when another infection is already raging.
plos-pone-0011516: Rice carries a big family of cleanup enzymes that neutralize harmful aldehydes. This research paper maps the whole ALDH clan in rice with protein models, teasing out how the members differ in shape and job. The catalog helps crop scientists grasp how rice weathers stress — and how to breed hardier plants.
plos-pone-0011616: Why do some Senegalese children suffer malaria attacks while others shrug off infection? This genome-wide linkage study scans a 250K SNP map for DNA regions tied to Plasmodium falciparum infection and mild malaria. The genetic landmarks point to inherited factors in the fight against the deadliest malaria.
plos-pone-0011716: Leukemia cells of the chronic lymphocytic type follow chemical trails laid by CXCL12/CXCR4 signals. This research paper charts that signal network by reading protein phosphate tags across the cell. The wiring map shows what steers the cancer's movements — routes future drugs might cut.
plos-pone-0011816: Silkworm grubs make their blood cells in a special organ that runs two production lines. This research paper traces two separate blood-cell family lines in that organ. The double assembly line reveals how insects build their immune defenses from two blueprints.
plos-pone-0012016: Cell lines modeling the embryo's support tissues need comparing. This research paper performs a comparative analysis of extra-embryonic endoderm cell lines. The side-by-side study reveals which lines best model early development in the dish today and tomorrow.
plos-pone-0012116: White blood cells mature through teamwork among genes. This research paper reveals how gene groups move together during neutrophil development — genome vehicles at work. The vehicle idea reframes development as a convoy, not a solo trip today, but a parade.
plos-pone-0012216: A new image protocol tracks particles in living lymph nodes. This research paper tests a stacked difference image protocol for particle tracking in glow microscopy in mouse lymph nodes. The tracking protocol sharpens immune cell imaging, today and always, for good measure, worldwide.
plos-pone-0012316: Plant compounds moonlight as pain-enzyme helpers. This research paper shows certain bioflavonoids can serve as reducing helpers of cyclooxygenase I and II. The helper finding reveals flavonoid drug action, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012416: Botox antibodies tested — longer life, better therapy. This research paper tests Botox toxin-fighting antibodies and shows their half-lives shape treatment strength. The antibody testing reveals antitoxin design, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012516: Joint ultrasound linked to Th17 cells in arthritis. This research paper links power Doppler ultrasound to the presence of Th17 cells in the arthritis joint. The ultrasound-cell link reveals an arthritis-imaging biomarker, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012616: Methylation arrays sort breast cancer subtypes. This research paper uses array-based DNA methylation profiling for breast cancer subtype sorting. cotta-triall-of-witch-craft-english-1616:
John Cotta, a doctor of Northampton, published The Triall of Witch-craft in 1616. Rather than defend the accused, Cotta attacks the tests used to find witches. His method is a physician's skepticism, turned on the whole business of witch-finding in Jacobean England.

Swimming a suspect, hunting for devil's marks, and watching for familiars all fail his scrutiny. Such proofs, he argues, can brand the innocent as surely as the guilty. Cotta accepts that witchcraft exists, but demands evidence worthy of a court. His book is medicine enlisted against superstition. Doctors would cite it whenever weak tests sent neighbors to the gallows.
roberts-treatise-of-witchcraft-english-1:
Alexander Roberts, a minister, published his Treatise of Witchcraft in 1616, the same year as Cotta's skeptical Triall. Roberts takes the other road. His treatise lays down propositions on witchcraft, point by careful point, building an orderly rulebook for Jacobean readers.

Scripture anchors each proposition, and English cases fill out the doctrine. Roberts writes for the parish pulpit, clear and systematic. His book was meant to be preached from on Sundays. Set beside Cotta, it shows two English churchmen of one year facing opposite ways on evidence. Roberts represents the settled teaching that most Jacobean congregations actually heard about witches.
